before.content_html:
Dickens and the Class System

Charles Dickens published Great Expectations as a weekly serial in All the Year Round between December 1860 and August 1861. Victorian Britain was rigidly divided by class. At the top sat the aristocracy and landed gentry — families who inherited wealth. Below them, a growing middle class of merchants and lawyers aspired to climb higher. At the bottom, the working class struggled in conditions Dickens knew firsthand: when he was twelve, his father was imprisoned for debt, and young Charles was forced to work in a blacking factory.

This autobiography matters. Pip’s shame about his working-class origins, his desperate desire to become a gentleman, and his eventual realisation that wealth does not equal worth all mirror Dickens’s own complicated relationship with class.

Key Fact

Victorian society had three rigid tiers: aristocracy/gentry (inherited wealth), middle class (earned wealth), and working class/poor. Dickens drew on his own childhood poverty when creating Pip’s shame about his origins at the forge.

The ‘Gentleman’ Ideal

In Victorian culture, a gentleman was defined by wealth, education, manners, and the absence of manual labour. This ideal shaped everything from marriage prospects to legal rights.

Dickens uses Great Expectations to interrogate this ideal ruthlessly. Pip believes becoming a gentleman will make him worthy of Estella’s love. Instead, his ‘great expectations’ make him a snob — ashamed of Joe Gargery, the man who raised him with genuine kindness. The true gentleman of the novel is Joe himself: no wealth, no education, no status, but absolute moral integrity.

Compeyson and Magwitch committed the same crime, but at trial Compeyson — who dressed like a gentleman — received fourteen years while Magwitch received life. As Magwitch tells Pip: “I noticed first of all what a gentleman Compeyson looked, wi’ his curly hair and his black clothes and his white pocket handkerchief, and what a common sort of wretch I looked.” Same crime, different punishments — purely because of appearance and class.

Social Mobility and Self-Improvement

Victorian Britain offered limited pathways for social mobility. Samuel Smiles’s Self-Help (1859) promoted the idea that effort could raise anyone. But Dickens complicates this: Pip’s rise is funded by a convict’s money, and his ‘improvement’ makes him worse — more snobbish, less kind.

Biddy represents genuine self-improvement. She educates herself, becoming a schoolteacher through intelligence and determination, without losing her kindness. Where Pip’s rise corrupts him, Biddy’s enriches her.

Key Fact

Dickens challenges the belief that social climbing equals moral improvement. Pip’s wealth makes him worse. Joe and Biddy — who remain working class — are the novel’s moral centres. True worth comes from character, not class.

Crime, Punishment, and the Law

The criminal justice system pervades the novel. It opens on the marshes near a prison hulk. Magwitch is an escaped prisoner. Jaggers washes his hands after dealing with criminals. Newgate Prison looms over London.

Transportation to penal colonies was a common sentence. Magwitch is transported for life; returning illegally risks hanging. Dickens exposes the brutal disproportion of Victorian punishment.

Dickens was the most popular novelist of his age. Serialised weekly, Great Expectations needed cliffhangers, but beyond entertainment Dickens wanted middle-class readers to question their assumptions. First-person narration forces the reader to share Pip’s shame, ambition, and painful realisation.

Structure: The Bildungsroman

The novel divides into three stages: Stage 1 (Chs 1–19) — childhood at the forge; Stage 2 (Chs 20–39) — gentleman in London; Stage 3 (Chs 40–59) — disillusionment and moral recovery. The structure mirrors innocence, corruption, and redemption.

Dickens uses first-person retrospective narration. The adult Pip looks back with regret and wisdom, commenting on his younger self’s mistakes even as we experience them.

before.content_html:
The Opening: Pip and the Convict

Great Expectations opens in a graveyard on the Kent marshes. The young orphan Pip is visiting his parents’ graves when a terrifying convict — Abel Magwitch — seizes him and demands food and a file to remove his leg-iron. Pip is “a small bundle of shivers growing afraid of it all and beginning to cry.” The opening establishes two things that drive the entire novel: Pip’s vulnerability and his first moral choice.

Pip steals food and a file from his sister’s kitchen and brings them to Magwitch. This act of terrified kindness becomes the foundation of the plot. Magwitch never forgets it. Years later, transported to Australia, he devotes his life to making Pip a gentleman — repaying the child who showed him humanity when no one else would. Dickens plants the seed of the novel’s central irony here: Pip’s ‘great expectations’ originate in an act of compassion, yet they ultimately corrupt him.

Key Fact

The graveyard opening establishes Pip’s isolation (orphan among tombstones), introduces the convict Magwitch, and triggers the central irony: Pip’s act of compassion eventually funds the ‘great expectations’ that corrupt him.

Life at the Forge

Pip is “brought up by hand” by his sister, Mrs Joe Gargery, a phrase Dickens uses with dark irony — it means both bottle-fed (Mrs Joe is not his mother) and physically beaten. Mrs Joe is harsh, resentful, and violent, wielding a cane she calls Tickler. In contrast, her husband Joe is Pip’s protector and companion. Joe is a blacksmith — strong, gentle, uneducated, and utterly loyal. He tells Pip: “we’d be good pals, wouldn’t us, Pip? If it warn’t for your sister.”

The forge represents honest labour, warmth, and simple goodness. Pip is happy there — or at least content — until Satis House introduces him to a world of wealth and refinement that makes him despise his own home. Dickens establishes the forge as a moral touchstone: Pip’s journey away from it is a journey away from goodness, and his return at the end signals moral recovery.

Mrs Joe’s violence towards Pip and Joe is presented with grim humour — Tickler is almost a comic prop — but Dickens is showing something real. Victorian children had few legal protections; physical punishment was normal and expected. Mrs Joe resents being ‘burdened’ with Pip, and her anger reflects the limited options available to working-class women. She is later attacked by Orlick, struck with a convict’s leg-iron, leaving her brain-damaged and dependent. Dickens’s treatment of her is complex: she is both a victim of her circumstances and a source of suffering for Pip and Joe.

Satis House: Pip’s World Transformed

When Pip is summoned to Satis House to “play” for the wealthy Miss Havisham, his entire sense of self is shattered. Satis House is a decaying mansion where time has stopped: the clocks are frozen at twenty to nine, the wedding breakfast rots on the table, and Miss Havisham wears her yellowed bridal dress. She was jilted on her wedding day by the swindler Compeyson and has never recovered.

Miss Havisham has adopted Estella and raised her as a weapon of revenge against men. Estella is beautiful, cold, and cruel. She humiliates Pip immediately: “He calls the knaves, Jacks, this boy! And what coarse hands he has! And what thick boots!” Before this moment, Pip had never felt ashamed of who he was. After it, he is consumed by shame. He tells us: “I took the opportunity of being alone in the courtyard, to look at my coarse hands and my common boots. They had never troubled me before, but they troubled me now.”

Key Fact

Estella’s class-based humiliation (‘coarse hands’, ‘thick boots’, ‘knaves’ vs ‘Jacks’) transforms Pip’s self-image. For the first time, he feels ashamed of his class — and this shame drives the entire plot. He begins to desire a life of wealth and refinement, rejecting the forge and everything Joe represents.

Miss Havisham’s Manipulation

Miss Havisham uses both Pip and Estella as instruments of her revenge. She encourages Pip’s infatuation with Estella, watching with satisfaction as Estella’s cruelty causes him pain. “Break their hearts, my pride and hope,” she tells Estella, “break their hearts and have no mercy!” Miss Havisham has taught Estella to be incapable of love — a fact that will eventually rebound on Miss Havisham herself when Estella cannot love her either.

Pip mistakenly believes Miss Havisham is his secret benefactor and that she intends him to marry Estella. This assumption — based entirely on class prejudice (he cannot imagine a convict as a benefactor) — is the novel’s great dramatic irony.

After visiting Satis House, Pip begins to lie. He tells Mrs Joe and Pumblechook fantastic stories about Miss Havisham’s house — claiming they played with flags and swords and that she sat in a velvet coach. Only to Joe does he confess the truth: “I wished Joe had been rather more genteelly brought up, and then I should have been so too.” This is the first sign of Pip’s snobbery. He does not wish Joe were kinder or wiser — he wishes Joe were more ‘genteel.’ His values have already begun to shift from moral worth to social status.

The Seeds of Discontent

By the end of Stage 1, Pip is apprenticed to Joe as a blacksmith — a future that once seemed natural and good. But now he calls the forge “coarse and common” and his life there a source of “mortification.” He tells us: “I used to want — quite painfully — to be a gentleman.” The repetition of ‘common’ throughout these chapters is deliberate: Dickens shows how Estella’s single word of class contempt has colonised Pip’s entire way of seeing himself and his world.

before.content_html:
Pip’s Moral Recovery

After the shock of Magwitch’s revelation, Pip begins a slow moral transformation. He stops seeing Magwitch as a class category and starts seeing him as a human being. He learns Magwitch’s tragic life story — orphaned, starved, criminalised from childhood — and feels “a new affection” for the old convict. This shift is the novel’s emotional turning point: Pip’s recovery begins when he stops judging people by their class and starts judging them by their character.

Pip’s first act of genuine selflessness is his plan to help Magwitch escape England. He enlists Herbert Pocket’s help to row Magwitch down the Thames to a ship bound for Europe. This is not about money or status — Pip risks his own freedom to save the man he once despised. Dickens shows that real gentlemanliness is not about manners or wealth; it is about moral courage and compassion.

Key Fact

Pip’s moral recovery begins when he sees Magwitch as a person rather than a class category. His plan to help Magwitch escape — risking his own freedom — is his first genuinely selfless act, proving that true gentlemanliness is about compassion, not status.

The Escape Attempt

Pip, Herbert, and Startop row Magwitch down the Thames in Chapter 54. The escape fails. Compeyson — Magwitch’s old enemy — has informed on them. As the customs boat bears down, Magwitch and Compeyson struggle in the water. Compeyson drowns. Magwitch is recaptured, badly injured, and sentenced to death.

The escape sequence is Dickens at his most cinematic. The river journey, conducted in whispers and tension, contrasts with the violent climax. Structurally, the Thames functions as both physical escape route and symbolic journey: Pip is attempting to free Magwitch from the system that has always oppressed him, just as he himself is finally breaking free from the class prejudice that has oppressed his moral development.

Magwitch dies in prison before his execution can take place. In his final moments, Pip holds his hand and tells him that his daughter — Estella — is alive, beautiful, and a lady. Magwitch’s face softens: “You had a child once, whom you loved and lost… She lived and found powerful friends. She is living now. She is a lady and very beautiful. And I love her!” This scene is deeply moving because it shows Pip’s transformation is complete. He is no longer ashamed of Magwitch. He gives the dying man the only comfort he can — the knowledge that his daughter survived.

Joe’s Return and Pip’s Illness

After Magwitch’s death, Pip falls desperately ill with fever and debt. He is arrested and imprisoned. In his delirium, he keeps calling for Joe — and Joe comes. Without reproach, without a word of recrimination, Joe nurses Pip back to health. He pays Pip’s debts. He sits by his bedside day and night. When Pip recovers, Joe quietly slips away before Pip can thank him properly, leaving only a note.

This scene mirrors the novel’s opening: once again, Pip is helpless and Joe is his rescuer. But now Pip understands what Joe’s love means. He has spent the entire novel trying to become a gentleman — and the most genuinely gentle man in his life was there all along, at the forge, asking nothing in return. Joe’s unconditional love is the moral standard against which all other characters are measured.

Key Fact

Joe nurses Pip without reproach, pays his debts, and leaves without seeking thanks. His unconditional love — consistent from the first chapter to the last — is the novel’s definition of true gentlemanliness: moral worth that exists entirely independent of wealth or class.

The Two Endings

Dickens originally wrote a bleak ending in which Pip encounters Estella briefly in London. She has remarried after Drummle’s death, and they part as strangers. But his friend Bulwer-Lytton persuaded him to revise it. In the published ending, Pip returns to Satis House (now demolished) and finds Estella there. She has been “bent and broken” by suffering, and the final line is deliberately ambiguous: “I saw no shadow of another parting from her.”

The ambiguity of the revised ending is crucial. It can be read as hopeful (they stay together) or melancholy (Pip’s delusion continues). Dickens may have intended both readings simultaneously. The original ending is arguably more consistent with the novel’s themes: Pip’s expectations were always misguided, and a fairy-tale union with Estella would undermine that message.

Before the Estella scene, Pip returns to the forge hoping to marry Biddy — only to discover that she has married Joe. This final humbling is Dickens’s last lesson for Pip: he cannot simply ‘claim’ the good people he neglected. Joe and Biddy have found happiness together without him. Pip must accept the consequences of his choices. He goes abroad with Herbert to work honestly in business — finally earning his way rather than living off someone else’s money.

before.content_html:
Pip: The Flawed Narrator

Pip is both the novel’s protagonist and its most deeply flawed character. As a child, he is innocent, compassionate, and loyal — he helps Magwitch out of genuine fear and pity. But once Estella humiliates him at Satis House, his values shift from moral worth to social status. He becomes a snob, treating Joe with “a touch of reproach” and calling the forge “coarse and common.”

Dickens uses first-person retrospective narration to brilliant effect. The adult Pip narrates with self-awareness and regret, commenting on his younger self’s foolishness even as we experience it. This double perspective means the reader both identifies with Pip’s desires and recognises their destructiveness. Pip is not a villain — he is a cautionary tale about what happens when a fundamentally decent person internalises the wrong values.

Key Fact

Pip’s arc moves through three phases: innocent child (forge), corrupted gentleman (London), and redeemed adult (after Magwitch). The retrospective narration means the adult Pip judges his younger self, creating a dual perspective that invites both sympathy and criticism.

Estella: Made, Not Born

Estella is Miss Havisham’s weapon — raised to “break their hearts and have no mercy.” She tells Pip with chilling honesty: “I have no heart — if that has anything to do with my memory.” She is not naturally cruel; she has been made cruel. Dickens presents her as both perpetrator and victim: she inflicts pain on Pip but is herself a victim of Miss Havisham’s manipulation.

Estella’s marriage to the brutal Bentley Drummle — chosen precisely because he will make her suffer — extends her self-destructive conditioning. In the published ending, suffering has “bent and broken” her into someone capable of empathy. This raises a troubling question: does Dickens suggest that women must suffer to become fully human? Or is he showing that Miss Havisham’s emotional abuse has consequences that take a lifetime to undo?

Estella’s true identity — daughter of the convict Magwitch and the accused murderer Molly — demolishes the class system’s logic. She was raised as an aristocratic lady, yet her blood is as ‘common’ as Pip’s. Dickens’s point: class is performance, not essence. Estella’s refinement is no more innate than Pip’s. Both are constructed identities built on deception.

Miss Havisham: Victim and Villain

Miss Havisham was jilted on her wedding day by the swindler Compeyson. She stopped all the clocks at twenty to nine, left the wedding breakfast to rot, and never removed her bridal dress. She adopted Estella specifically to use as an instrument of revenge against men. She manipulates Pip, encouraging his love for Estella while knowing it will never be returned.

Yet Dickens also presents her as a victim. She was defrauded of her money and her happiness by a man who exploited her trust. Her monomania — her total fixation on her betrayal — has consumed her identity. When she finally realises the damage she has done to Estella (who cannot love even her), she is overwhelmed with remorse: “What have I done! What have I done!” Her dress catches fire and she burns — a fitting symbolic death for a character consumed by her own destructive passions.

Key Fact

Miss Havisham is both villain (manipulates Pip, weaponises Estella, ‘break their hearts’) and victim (jilted by Compeyson, trapped by monomania, ultimately consumed by remorse). Her death by fire symbolises the self-destructive nature of revenge.

Magwitch: The Hidden Heart

Magwitch begins the novel as a terrifying figure: a “fearful man, all in coarse grey, with a great iron on his leg.” By the end, he is one of its most sympathetic characters. His life story — orphaned, starved, “in jail and out of jail” — reveals that Victorian society created the criminal it then punished. His love for Pip is genuine, selfless, and transformative. Dickens uses Magwitch to argue that moral worth has nothing to do with class or criminal record.

Joe Gargery is the novel’s moral touchstone. His qualities — loyalty, kindness, forgiveness, honesty — never change. He nurses Pip through illness, pays his debts, and never reproaches him. Joe’s discomfort in London (fidgeting with his hat, calling Pip “Sir”) is not inferiority but integrity: he refuses to pretend to be something he is not. Biddy is Joe’s intellectual equal, perceptive and honest. She sees through Pip’s snobbery before he does: “Are you quite sure, then, that you WILL come to see him often?” she asks, knowing the answer. Together, Joe and Biddy represent everything Pip should value but doesn’t — until it is almost too late.

Jaggers and Wemmick: The System’s Price

Jaggers and Wemmick show the psychological cost of operating within a corrupt system. Jaggers’s hand-washing ritual symbolises his attempt to cleanse himself of moral contamination. Wemmick’s split personality (mechanical clerk by day, warm castle-dweller by night) shows how London forces people to compartmentalise their humanity. Together, they demonstrate that the Victorian legal and social system damages everyone it touches, not just the poor.

before.content_html:
Theme: Class and the Gentleman Ideal

The central theme of Great Expectations is the relationship between class and moral worth. Dickens dismantles the Victorian gentleman ideal through a sustained contrast: characters with wealth and status (Compeyson, Drummle, Miss Havisham) are morally corrupt, while characters without status (Joe, Biddy, Magwitch) demonstrate genuine goodness. Pip’s journey — from content working-class child to corrupted gentleman to redeemed adult — is Dickens’s argument in narrative form.

Key quotation: Magwitch’s declaration — “I’ve made a gentleman on you!” — is loaded with irony. Magwitch has funded Pip’s transformation, but Pip is no gentleman in the moral sense. The convict’s money bought clothes, education, and manners, but it could not buy character. That, Dickens shows, can only come from within.

Key Fact

Dickens argues that class and moral worth are unrelated. Wealthy characters (Compeyson, Drummle) are corrupt; working-class characters (Joe, Biddy) are good. Pip’s arc proves that becoming a gentleman in social terms can make you worse in moral terms.

Theme: Guilt and Conscience

Guilt pervades the novel. Pip feels guilty for helping a convict, for being ashamed of Joe, for his wasted opportunities, and for his treatment of those who love him. The adult narrator’s tone is suffused with remorse. His guilt drives the plot: it is guilt that makes him help Magwitch escape; it is guilt that sends him back to the forge; it is guilt that shapes his narration.

Miss Havisham’s guilt also transforms her. When she finally sees that Estella cannot love even her, she is consumed by remorse: “What have I done!” Her death by fire can be read as symbolic punishment for her sins — or as the only possible release from guilt that has consumed her entirely.

Dickens blurs the line between criminal and innocent. Magwitch is a convicted criminal but morally generous. Compeyson is a ‘gentleman’ but a swindler. Pip has committed no crime but is morally guilty of snobbery and ingratitude. Jaggers handles criminals all day but arranges Estella’s adoption to save her. Dickens argues that legal guilt and moral guilt are separate categories — and that Victorian society confuses the two.

Theme: Identity and Self-Knowledge

Great Expectations is fundamentally a novel about identity. Pip spends most of the novel trying to become someone he is not. His constructed identity as a ‘gentleman’ is a performance funded by criminal money. Estella’s identity as a ‘lady’ is a performance maintained by secrecy. Miss Havisham’s identity as a jilted bride is a performance frozen in time.

Only the characters who are authentically themselves — Joe, Biddy, Herbert — are happy. Dickens’s message is clear: self-knowledge comes not from acquiring a new identity but from stripping away false ones. Pip must lose his wealth, his status, and his illusions before he can see clearly who he is and what matters.

Key Fact

Pip (performing gentleman), Estella (performing lady), and Miss Havisham (performing jilted bride) all construct false identities. Joe is the only major character who is wholly authentic. Dickens argues that self-knowledge requires stripping away performance and facing truth.

Theme: Redemption and Forgiveness

The novel offers redemption to those who earn it. Pip is redeemed through suffering, humility, and genuine compassion for Magwitch. Miss Havisham achieves partial redemption through her agonised remorse, though too late to undo the damage. Even Estella, “bent and broken” by her marriage to Drummle, becomes capable of empathy.

Joe embodies forgiveness. He never reproaches Pip for years of neglect and snobbery. His unconditional love is the moral standard against which all other relationships are measured. Dickens suggests that redemption is always possible — but it requires genuine moral change, not just regret.

Your 19th-century novel question may offer a choice between an extract-based task and a discursive task. Extract-based: you are given a passage and must analyse it closely, then connect to the whole text. Focus on language (AO2) first, then widen to themes and context. Discursive: you respond to a statement (for example, ‘How far do you agree?’). Structure an argument with multiple paragraphs, each focusing on a different aspect. Both require AO1 (response with textual references), AO2 (analysis of language/form/structure), and AO3 (context). Plan carefully and manage your time — check your exam board’s specimen paper for exact weightings and timings.

Structuring an Analytical Response

A strong response has: (1) a clear opening that addresses the question directly; (2) several analytical paragraphs, each with a point, evidence (quotation), analysis of language/method, and contextual link; (3) a brief conclusion that returns to the question. For AO2, zoom in on individual words and techniques. For AO3, embed context within your analysis rather than bolting it on as a separate paragraph. The best responses are exploratory, considering alternative interpretations.
before.exam_tip_html: Remember: OCR marks AO1, AO2, and AO3 together in a holistic band. You do not get separate marks for each AO. This means every paragraph should blend response, language analysis, and context seamlessly. Practise writing paragraphs that do all three at once.
